# **How Claims History Affects Your Insurance Rates (And What You Can Actually Do About It)**


Your claims history determines your insurance costs, as each filed claim impacts your rates for years.


Understanding how carriers evaluate claims history and when to file versus pay out of pocket helps you make strategic decisions that protect both your coverage and your wallet.


[Harper](https://www.harperinsure.com/) helps business owners understand their loss runs, which are reports showing their history of insurance claims, and implement strategies to improve insurability while maintaining necessary protection.


## **How Long Do Claims Stay On Your Insurance Record?**


Claims remain on your insurance record for different time periods depending on the type of coverage and state regulations. Understanding these timeframes helps you anticipate when rate increases will decrease.


### **Auto Insurance Claims**


Auto insurance claims typically stay on your record for[three to five years](https://www.dgglaw.com/car-accidents-stay-on-insurance/) . According to industry data, most insurance companies review the past three to five years when calculating rates.


The clock starts from the date of the accident, not the date the claim was resolved.


Some states maintain driving records for longer periods, but insurers generally consider only the most recent 3 to 5 years when pricing policies.


### **Homeowners Insurance Claims**


Home insurance claims stay on your record between **five and seven years** . The Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange (CLUE), a database that tracks your history of home insurance claims, stores seven years of claim records that insurance companies review when underwriting policies.


This shared database means claims follow you even when switching insurers.


New carriers see your complete claims history regardless of which company you filed with previously.


### **Commercial Insurance Claims**


Business insurance claims remain on loss runs, detailed reports showing a company's history of insurance claims for **five to seven years** .


Carriers typically review five years of these loss history reports when underwriting commercial policies, though some examine up to seven years for certain coverage types.


Multiple claims within this lookback period significantly impact your ability to obtain coverage and the rates carriers offer.


## **Understanding Loss Runs And How Carriers Use Them**


Loss runs are detailed claims history reports that carriers use to evaluate risk and determine pricing. These documents contain critical information that insurers review during underwriting.


### **What Loss Runs Include**


Loss runs document every claim filed under your policies. Each entry lists:


- The date of the incident
- The type of claim
- The amount paid or set aside for payment (reserved)
- Whether the claim is still active (open) or completed (closed)
- A description of what happened


Carriers examine loss run patterns to identify risk trends. Frequent small claims often signal a higher risk than a single large claim because they indicate ongoing operational issues.


### **How Carriers Evaluate Claims History**


Insurance companies use sophisticated algorithms to evaluate claims frequency, severity, and recency.


**Recent claims carry more weight than older incidents.** Claims within the past year impact rates more than those from four years ago.


**Claim frequency matters more than individual severity** for many carriers. Three small claims totaling $15,000 often result in higher rate increases than a single $30,000 claim because multiple claims suggest persistent risk management problems.


At-fault versus not-at-fault claims also influence pricing.[Research](https://consumerfed.org/press_release/major-insurance-companies-raise-premiums-not-fault-accidents/) shows that while major insurance companies may raise premiums after not-at-fault accidents, at-fault collisions lead to significantly higher rate increases.


However, even not-at-fault claims can trigger rate increases as they demonstrate overall risk exposure.


### **Industry-Wide Claim Databases**


CLUE reports track property and auto claims across all carriers. Insurers share claim information through this database maintained by LexisNexis.


When you apply for new coverage, carriers access your complete CLUE report, which shows all claims filed within the past seven years, regardless of which company insured you.


This industry-wide sharing means you cannot escape claims history by switching carriers. Your record follows you across the entire insurance marketplace.


## **How Claims Impact Your Insurance Rates**


The financial impact of filing claims extends beyond the immediate claim payment. Rate increases following claims often exceed the claim amount over time.


### **Average Rate Increases After Claims**


According to[Bankrate's 2025 insurance analysis](https://www.bankrate.com/insurance/car/rates-after-an-accident/) , drivers with a single at-fault accident pay **43% more for full coverage than** drivers with clean records.


The average cost of full-coverage car insurance nationwide reached **$2,638 in 2025** , up **12% from 2024,** according to Bankrate research.


Rate increases from accidents typically persist for three to five years from the date of the incident. After this period without new claims or violations, drivers generally see premiums return to pre-accident levels.


### **Duration Of Rate Increases**


Rate increases typically last three to five years, matching the lookback period carriers use.


According to industry research, insurance rates generally decrease once accidents fall off your record. After three years without new claims or violations, drivers typically see premiums return to pre-accident levels.


Some insurers gradually lower rates each year without incidents, while others adjust premiums only when claims fully drop off the review period.


### **Cumulative Impact Of Multiple Claims**


Multiple claims within the review period compound rate increases exponentially.


Each additional claim signals higher risk, leading to steeper premium adjustments than a single claim would on its own.


Carriers may also decline to renew policies or refuse to issue new coverage when claims frequency exceeds acceptable thresholds. Three or more claims within five years often trigger non-renewal regardless of claim size.


## **When To Pay Out-Of-Pocket Versus Filing A Claim**


Strategic claim filing decisions require weighing immediate repair costs against long-term rate impacts. Not every loss warrants filing a claim.


### **Calculating The True Cost Of Filing**


The true cost of filing a claim extends far beyond the immediate repair benefit you receive. You must factor in your deductible, which you pay regardless, plus the cumulative premium increases over the following years.


**Consider this framework:** Subtract your deductible from the total repair cost to find your net insurance benefit. Then calculate the percentage increase applied to your current premium and multiply by the duration of the increase (typically three to five years).


If your total increased premiums over this period exceed your net insurance benefit, paying out-of-pocket saves money long-term.


The math often shows that smaller claims cost more in premium increases than they provide in immediate benefits, making self-payment the financially superior choice.


### **Claim Threshold Guidelines**


Insurance professionals commonly recommend using your annual premium as a baseline for claim decisions.


**General principle:** Consider self-insuring for repairs costing less than twice your annual premium.


This threshold accounts for the multi-year impact of rate increases following claims. The long-term rate impact often exceeds short-term savings from filing smaller claims.


Your specific threshold may vary based on your current rates, claims history, and your carrier's rate-increase patterns. Drivers with clean records and lower premiums can afford to self-pay larger claims than those already facing elevated rates.


### **Situations Where You Should Always File**


Certain circumstances require filing claims regardless of cost considerations:


- **Third parties are involved** , even if the damages appear minor (injuries may not manifest immediately)
- **Damages exceed your financial capacity** to repair out-of-pocket
- **Liability exposure from injuries** or significant property damage creates legal risk
- **Total losses** where repair costs approach or exceed vehicle or property value


Missing coverage deadlines by attempting out-of-pocket repairs that prove inadequate leaves you unprotected.


## **Strategies To Improve Your Insurability After Claims**


Claims history cannot be erased, but specific actions improve your insurance profile and reduce long-term rate impacts.


### **Maintain A Clean Record Going Forward**


Avoiding additional claims, tickets, and violations represents your most effective strategy.


Each claim-free year strengthens your insurability and qualifies you for better rates.


Carriers offer claim-free discounts that reward safe operation over time. According to industry data, after three years without new claims or violations, drivers typically see their premiums return to pre-accident levels.


### **Take Defensive Driving Courses**


Many insurance companies offer discounts for completing approved safety courses.


Defensive driving courses demonstrate a commitment to risk reduction and may offset rate increases resulting from prior claims.


Check with your carrier about specific course requirements and available discounts before enrolling.


### **Increase Your Deductibles**


Higher deductibles reduce premiums while discouraging small claim filings.


According to the[Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/nine-ways-to-lower-your-auto-insurance-costs) , a $1,000 increase in comprehensive or collision deductibles can lead to **40% savings** on those coverage components.


Ensure you maintain adequate reserves to cover higher deductibles when losses occur. Savings from lower premiums should fund your deductible reserve account.


### **Shop Multiple Carriers**


Insurance companies weigh claims history differently. Carrier A might penalize two claims more heavily than Carrier B based on their underwriting models and risk appetite.


Comparing quotes from at least five insurers helps identify carriers offering competitive rates despite your claims history.


Work with independent brokers who access multiple insurance markets, rather than captive agents representing a single carrier.


### **Bundle Multiple Policies**


Combining auto and home insurance or multiple business policies with one carrier often yields multi-policy discounts.


These discounts may offset portions of rate increases from claims history.


Bundling also simplifies claims management and may qualify you for forgiveness programs offered by some carriers to loyal customers.


## **Understanding Accident Forgiveness Programs**


Accident forgiveness prevents first-time claims from affecting your rates. These programs represent valuable protection for drivers and policyholders with clean records.


### **How Accident Forgiveness Works**


Carriers offering accident forgiveness won't increase your rates after your first at-fault accident. This benefit protects the rate structure you had before the claim occurred.


Forgiveness typically applies only to at-fault auto accidents, not all claim types.


It usually covers one accident per policy period or per driver on the policy.


### **Who Offers Accident Forgiveness**


Most major carriers offer accident forgiveness through different structures:


- **Allstate** : Sign up when you start your policy
- **Farmers** : Forgives one at-fault accident for every three years without an accident
- **Progressive** : Free forgiveness for[claims under $500](https://www.progressive.com/answers/what-is-accident-forgiveness/) , with expanded forgiveness as a loyalty perk
- **GEICO** : Free to loyal customers or premium versions for purchase
- **Nationwide** : Extends to every driver on a policy (one forgiven accident per policy)


Some offer free accident forgiveness as a loyalty reward after a claim-free period. Others offer it as an optional policy add-on for an additional premium.


### **Requirements And Limitations**


Accident forgiveness typically requires maintaining a clean record for a specified period before qualifying.


Most carriers require **three to five claim-free years** before enrolling you in free forgiveness programs.


Forgiveness doesn't apply to multiple accidents within policy periods. If you have two at-fault accidents in one year, only the first receives forgiveness while the second triggers rate increases.


Some carriers reset forgiveness benefits after use, requiring another clean period before forgiveness becomes available again.


## **How Different Claim Types Affect Rates Differently**


Not all claims carry equal weight in carrier underwriting models. Understanding how different claim types impact rates helps you make strategic decisions.


### **Property Damage Claims**


Property damage claims typically result in moderate rate increases compared to injury claims.


Carriers view property damage as less risky than bodily injury exposure because property damage is more predictable and controllable.


However, multiple property claims within review periods still trigger significant rate adjustments as they demonstrate ongoing risk management failures.


### **Bodily Injury Claims**


Bodily injury claims result in the highest rate increases because they involve unpredictable medical costs, lost wages, and pain and suffering damages that can balloon into six or seven figures.


According to[LexisNexis 2025 Auto Insurance Trends Report](https://risk.lexisnexis.com/about-us/press-room/press-release/20250612-us-auto-insurance-trends-report) , bodily injury severity jumped **9.2% year over year** .


These elevated claim costs drive carriers to significantly increase premiums after bodily injury claims.


### **Comprehensive Versus Collision Claims**


Comprehensive claims for theft, vandalism, weather, and animal strikes typically result in smaller rate increases than collision claims from at-fault accidents.


Comprehensive claims demonstrate less control over circumstances than collision accidents.


Some carriers don't increase rates for single comprehensive claims, particularly those involving acts of nature beyond the policyholder's control.


### **Liability Claims Where You're At Fault**


At-fault liability claims generate the steepest rate increases because they indicate a higher risk of future claims.


Carriers' price policies are based on expected claim frequency and severity.


At-fault accidents statistically predict a higher likelihood of future at-fault accidents. This correlation drives substantial rate adjustments lasting throughout the review period.


## **State-Specific Claim Regulations And Impacts**


State regulations influence how claims affect rates and how long impacts last. Understanding your state's rules helps anticipate rate changes.


### **States With Rate Increase Restrictions**


Some states prohibit insurers from increasing rates after certain types of claims.


**California** prohibits rate increases following not-at-fault accidents. This consumer protection prevents drivers from being penalized for incidents they didn't cause.


Other states limit the percentage increases carriers can apply following claims. These rate caps provide consumer protection while allowing insurers to adjust pricing based on risk.


### **States With Extended Review Periods And Minimum Requirements**


Certain states require carriers to review longer claim histories when underwriting. These extended lookback periods mean claims affect your rates for longer durations in those jurisdictions.


States requiring higher minimum liability coverage experience different claim patterns and rate adjustments than states with lower minimums. California, Virginia, and Utah recently increased minimum insurance requirements.


These regulatory changes affect overall market pricing beyond individual claims history because carriers adjust base rates to reflect higher mandatory coverage levels.


Verify your state's specific regulations and typical carrier practices when evaluating how long claims will impact your premiums.

- Others focus on preferred risks

### **Presenting Your Risk Effectively**


Brokers help you present your claims history in context. Simply submitting loss runs without explanation positions you negatively.


Brokers provide a narrative explaining:


- The circumstances of each claim
- The corrective actions implemented since the claims occurred
- Risk management improvements that reduce future claim likelihood
- Documentation of enhanced safety protocols and training


This strategic presentation helps underwriters evaluate your risk beyond raw claim counts, potentially securing better rates than applying directly to carriers.


### **Identifying Specialty Markets**


Some carriers specialize in higher-risk insureds or specific claim scenarios.


Standard carriers may decline or quote prohibitive rates for insureds with multiple claims, but specialty markets offer coverage at reasonable prices.


Brokers maintain relationships with these specialty carriers and know when to approach them rather than continue marketing your risk in standard markets.


## **Long-Term Strategies For Claims Management**


Proactive claims management minimizes both claim frequency and the long-term rate impacts of necessary claims.


### **Implementing Risk Management Programs**


Formal risk management programs demonstrate commitment to loss prevention:


- Document safety training programs
- Maintain regular equipment maintenance schedules
- Establish incident investigation procedures
- Create corrective action implementation processes


Carriers view comprehensive risk management programs favorably during underwriting. These documented efforts may mitigate rate increases stemming from prior claims by showing you've addressed the root causes.


### **Regular Policy Reviews**


Annual insurance reviews identify coverage gaps and rate optimization opportunities.


Work with your broker to:


- Review loss runs
- Analyze claim trends
- Adjust deductibles based on claim experience
- Verify adequate coverage limits protecting your assets


Proactive reviews prevent coverage gaps and ensure you're not overpaying for insurance given your current risk profile.


### **Documentation And Incident Response**


Proper claim documentation affects both claim outcomes and how carriers view your risk management capabilities.


Best practices include:


- Maintain detailed incident reports
- Photograph damage immediately
- Document witness statements
- Preserve evidence supporting your position


Strong documentation may reduce claim severity and demonstrate your professionalism to carriers reviewing your loss history.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **How Long Do Auto Insurance Claims Stay On My Record?**


Auto insurance claims typically stay on your record for three to five years from the date of the accident. Most insurance companies review this timeframe when calculating rates. The exact duration depends on your state and carrier policies. Some states maintain driving records longer, but insurers generally consider only the most recent 3 to 5 years.


### **Can I Remove A Claim From My Insurance Record?**


You cannot remove legitimate claims from your insurance record. Claims remain in industry databases like CLUE for five to seven years regardless of carrier changes. However, you can dispute inaccurate claim information if errors exist in your records. Contact your insurance company and the CLUE database administrator to correct factual errors.


### **Do All Claims Increase My Insurance Rates?**


Not all claims result in rate increases, but most do. Comprehensive claims for weather damage or theft may not increase rates with some carriers. Small claims of $500 or less may qualify for accident forgiveness with certain insurers. However, at-fault collisions and liability claims almost always trigger rate increases. The severity of the increase depends on claim type, amount, and your prior claims history.


### **Should I File A Claim For Minor Damage?**


Calculate the true cost before filing minor damage claims. Compare your deductible plus three to five years of anticipated rate increases against the repair cost. If the claim benefit exceeds long-term rate impacts, file the claim. Generally, consider paying out of pocket for damage costing less than twice your annual premium, unless injuries or third-party liability are involved.


### **How Do Multiple Claims Affect My Rates?**


Multiple claims compound rate increases exponentially. Each additional claim during the review period signals higher risk, leading to steeper premium adjustments. Three or more claims within five years often trigger policy non-renewal or coverage declination when shopping for new insurance. Claim frequency matters more than severity for most carriers.


### **Do Not-At-Fault Accidents Increase My Rates?**


Yes, even not-at-fault accidents can increase your rates, though typically less than at-fault incidents. Average rates after not-at-fault accidents are $1,766 annually, compared with $2,539 for at-fault accidents and $1,638 for clean records. Some states, such as California, prohibit rate increases for at-fault accidents. Check your state regulations and carrier policies.


### **What Is Accident Forgiveness And How Does It Work?**


Accident forgiveness prevents your first at-fault accident from increasing your rates. Some carriers offer free forgiveness to loyal customers after claim-free periods. Others provide it as an optional policy add-on. Coverage typically applies to one accident per policy period. Requirements vary by carrier; most require three to five claim-free years to qualify for free forgiveness programs.
